messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj, a 32-year-old South Asian man married to his high school sweetheart, had been working steadily as a housekeeper at a local hotel for several years when he was mugged one late evening. The experience was so vivid that every detail remains seared into his memory. He recalls the dimly lit alleyway where the incident occurred and the sudden fear of being cornered by two men who demanded his wallet. Raj had felt helpless, pinned against a brick wall, as they snatched his belongings and left him alone in the darkness. Since then, Raj's memories have become hauntingly clear and detailed. Whenever he tries to describe what happened, he struggles to find the right words, feeling that any explanation falls short of conveying the depth of his experience. The physical pain associated with those memories is almost as real as if it were happening all over again. Each time a memory surfaces, Raj feels the same crushing pressure against his chest and the sharp ache in his wrists where he was held forcibly. Raj has come to believe that people are not what they seem, and this belief is deeply rooted in his experience of being robbed by those who appeared harmless at first glance. His distrust has grown stronger with each vivid recollection of that night, reinforcing his negative appraisals about the world's inherent danger and people’s untrustworthiness. His job as a housekeeper has become increasingly difficult due to these thoughts. He finds himself constantly on edge while working in empty rooms or hallways, wary of any shadowy figures he might encounter. Raj avoids certain areas where he feels more vulnerable, which has led to his supervisors giving him less desirable shifts and less interaction with regular guests. What frightens Raj most is that the world seems perpetually unsafe, and he can't shake the feeling that another attack could happen at any moment. This constant vigilance takes a toll on both his mental health and his marriage; he often cancels plans or declines social invitations out of fear of being caught off guard again. Despite his efforts to maintain a sense of normalcy, Raj's life has become increasingly isolated and tense. The vivid memories continue to haunt him, reinforcing the notion that everyone around him is potentially dangerous. This self-reinforcing cycle leaves him feeling trapped in a state of perpetual anxiety and distrust. It was this overwhelming fear and the realization that his daily functioning had been severely compromised that finally pushed Raj to seek help. He hopes to regain some sense of safety and trust, both in himself and in others. His primary concern is finding ways to manage his intrusive memories so that he can return to a life where he feels secure and connected once more.
